entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Thirty-First of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 144 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 115 · Saturday, the Thirty-First of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

144 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE PROCESSION DESK: THREE-QUARTERS OF A MILLION TURN OUT FOR THE CHAMPIONS — THE POLICE CALL IT PERHAPS THE LARGEST GATHERING IN WISCONSIN'S HISTORY, YOUNT RIDES IN ON UECKER'S HARLEY, AND FRELICK PLEDGES A HUNDRED THOUSAND BEERS

The procession this paper trailed yesterday morning came off grander than even Milwaukee dared forecast. By the constabulary's count more than 750,000 souls turned out for the parade and the rally that followed — a figure the police say may stand, their preliminary arithmetic suggests, as the largest crowd for a single day's event in the state's history.2 Fans staked their places along Wisconsin Avenue before dawn; by 8 o'clock thousands had already filled the lakefront grounds at Henry Maier Festival Park, where the 23,000-seat amphitheater held the rally and every stage on the 75 acres carried it by screen. The only prior parade in the club's annals, in 1982, honored a team that had lost the seventh game of the World's Series in St. Louis. This one, 44 years later, honored winners.

The rostrum ran long and merry. Robin Yount arrived astride Bob Uecker's Harley-Davidson, precisely as he did at the rally of 1982, and Ted Simmons spoke for the men of that older club; Rollie Fingers praised the bullpen and the scoreless-innings man Aaron Ashby by name. The Series' most valuable player William Contreras thanked the multitude in English; Brice Turang confessed what the final out had done to his nerves; the captain Christian Yelich called the day worth its long wait; and the hitting coach Daniel Vogelbach sang karaoke. The manager Pat Murphy rode the route at the parade's rear in a lawn chair with his children and quoted Bruce Springsteen from the stage, the owner Mark Attanasio pronounced the state's 6 million residents "one family" for the day, and the president of baseball operations Matt Arnold addressed the crowd with a beer in hand — a detail the crowd took as a credential. As for Sal Frelick, whose leap into the Lambeau stands this paper reported yesterday, he surveyed the sea of humanity and vowed to drink 100,000 beers in its honor — a program this desk neither endorses nor entirely doubts.2

THE OPTIONS LEDGER, SECOND DAY: TAMPA BAY TURNS LOOSE THE ARM THAT WON FIFTEEN AND THE GLOVE THAT ROAMED CENTER — WHILE BALTIMORE PAYS EFLIN TWO MILLIONS TO MEND HIS ELBOW ON THE OPEN MARKET

The settling of accounts that opened Thursday, as this paper's ledger recorded yesterday, ran through its second day without pause. The Gulf Coast club declined its mutual options on the pitcher Nick Martinez and the center fielder Cedric Mullins on Friday, loosing both to the market.3 Martinez, 36, gave Tampa Bay everything $9 million could reasonably buy — 15 wins against 6 defeats, a 3.10 earned-run average across 180 innings and 31 starts, and 16 October innings of five-run ball atop it — but the club chose the $4 million buyout over a $20 million encore, and the pitcher is reported to have declined his own half of the bargain in any case. Mullins required less deliberation: the one-time Oriole batted .205 with 15 home runs and 21 stolen bases in 137 games, and the half-million-dollar buyout was always the likelier end of his $10 million clause. The Tampa men must still rule on Drew Rasmussen's $20 million figure and a smaller one on the shortstop Taylor Walls before Monday.3

In Baltimore the ledger closed on Zach Eflin the way all parties expected: the Baltimores declined his $25 million mutual option and will pay the 32-year-old right-hander a $2 million buyout to seek his fortune on a mending elbow.4 Eflin's season amounted to one start — he left his debut on March 31 with elbow trouble and underwent the Tommy John operation on April 8 — yet he kept close to the club through his rehabilitation and professes a wish to return, so a reunion is not foreclosed. He joins a general exodus from the Baltimore rotation, Trevor Rogers, Chris Bassitt, Keegan Akin and Andrew Kittredge all likewise free, though the bullpen at least holds firm: Ryan Helsley chose the warm hearth on Thursday, as this paper set down yesterday, and the club has decisions yet to make on its outfielder Luis Robert Jr. and first baseman Ryan Mountcastle.4

THE APPOINTMENTS DESK: HOUSTON GOES TO THE CARDINALS' SCHOOLHOUSE FOR ITS NEW GENERAL MANAGER — FLORES, A LEFT-HANDER OF THREE-HUNDRED-AND-FIFTY GAMES IN HIS PITCHING DAYS, MUST FIRST FIND THE CLUB A MANAGER

The Houston nine filled their long-vacant front chair Friday night, naming Randy Flores general manager — the fourth such hire of the owner Jim Crane's tenure, and the end of a search that began when the club parted with Dana Brown better than two months ago.5 Flores, 51, comes from ten seasons in the St. Louis office, where he arrived in 2015 as director of scouting and served as an assistant general manager from 2019 onward. His is a varied résumé even by the modern front office's standards: a left-handed reliever in 350 major-league games for the Cardinals, Rockies, Rangers and Twins; a pitching coach at Southern California; a television analyst; the founder of a sports-video concern. "Randy has had a huge impact on the Cardinals over the last 10 seasons," said Crane, praising his new man's eye for talent.5

The work will not wait for the introductions, which come Monday at Daikin Park. The Astros won the American League West at 81-81 — an eighth divisional flag in ten seasons, and surely the least ornamented of the lot — and then declined to renew the manager Joe Espada after three seasons. Flores' first labor is therefore to find the club a manager, with a bench coach and sundry staff positions to fill behind him.5

THE FAR PACIFIC DESK: THE LOWEST EARNED-RUN FIGURE IN JAPAN ASKS FOR PASSAGE — SEIBU WILL POST THE RIGHT-HANDER TAIRA AND HIS 1.36, AND ALL THIRTY CLUBS GET FIVE-AND-FORTY DAYS TO BID

The winter market gains an arm from across the Pacific. The Saitama Seibu Lions announced they will approve the posting of the right-hander Kaima Taira, who led all of Nippon Professional Baseball in earned-run average this season — a 1.36 figure with a 0.96 WHIP across 23 games in his return to the rotation, after years of distinguished relief work that included a 1.71 average and 31 saves in 2025. Across eight NPB seasons the man's ledger reads 1.78.6 He turns 27 on November 15; once the posting is official, all 30 clubs will have a 45-day window to treat with him, with no restriction on the terms since he is past 25, and Seibu collecting a release fee scaled to whatever deal he strikes.

The scouts' reports read warmly: a fastball run up to the mid-to-upper 90s from a frame of just 5-foot-8, with a cutter, sweeper, changeup and splitter behind it, and a studious turn of mind toward the analytics besides.6 The skeptic's note concerns the frame — only Marcus Stroman, since Fred Norman in 1979, has pitched 100 innings in a season at that height or shorter, and some clubs will fancy Taira a reliever for exactly that reason, though his preference for starting may steer where he signs. He joins Teruaki Sato, the Hanshin Tigers slugger who took the Central League's Triple Crown, among the first NPB men seeking passage to these shores this winter.6

THE COMMERCE DESK: THE WINTER'S SECOND SWAP IS STRUCK FOR PLAIN COIN — DETROIT BUYS THE FOUR-TIMES-CLAIMED CHENG FROM BOSTON, AND THE WAIVER WIRE'S GREAT WANDERER GETS A PERCH

The winter's second trade followed its first by a single day, and was more modest still. Detroit on Friday acquired the infielder Tsung-Che Cheng from the Fenway men for cash considerations — the Bengals' first move of the offseason.7 Cheng, 25, a left-handed-hitting shortstop and second baseman from Taiwan who stands 5-foot-8, knows the waiver wire as a commuter knows his streetcar: cast off by Pittsburgh last offseason after five years in that system, he was claimed by the Rays, the Mets, the Nationals and the Red Sox inside a single month. Boston needed the roster room for men returning from the long infirmary list; Detroit paid cash rather than wait and bid against the wire.

The season past gave the little infielder his first major-league hit, on June 26 in his Boston debut, and a .256 average over 14 games in the big club's employ, with a .241/.345/.390 line and 8 home runs across 94 games at Worcester beneath it. In Detroit he finds a familiar face: the infielder Hao-Yu Lee, his countryman and teammate on the Chinese Taipei side at the World Baseball Classic, where Cheng reached base eight times in four games and stole four bags. The Bengals' own arithmetic now presses — 36 men on the roster of 40, with eight more to be accommodated off the 60-day infirmary list by Monday — so the wanderer's perch, it must be said, is not yet a guaranteed one.7

All Hallows' Eve, and for once the calendar's costume holiday finds the game with nothing left to disguise. The schedule page stands white this morning, as it will for 144 mornings more, until Opening Night restores the genuine article on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027.1 The Herald's lamps stay lit regardless: the options ledger runs through Monday,3 the awards season draws near, and the first arms from Japan are already asking for harbor. Let the neighborhood's small goblins have their evening — this desk has watched a Milwaukee club that spent fifty-seven seasons dressed as a contender finally take the mask off, and no store-bought fright will top it. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Thirtieth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 145 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 114 · Friday, the Thirtieth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

145 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE MARKET DESK: THE LAST OUT BARELY RECORDED AND THE WINTER BAZAAR THROWS OPEN ITS DOORS — KING DECLINES HIS OPTION AND WALKS OUT OF SAN DIEGO AS THE PRIZE ARM OF THE CLASS, AT TWO-AND-THIRTY

The World's Series ended Wednesday night; by Thursday the game had changed its business from pennants to purses. Michael King has declined the player option on his contract with the Padres, by the word of sources given to MLB.com, and steps onto the market as one of the foremost arms available entering his age-32 season. The right-hander earned the billing honestly in 2026 — a 3.21 earned-run average across 32 starts, worth a career-best 4.3 wins by the ledger's accounting — and salted his October with two starts of one run across 12 innings and 14 strikeouts, plus a two-inning save besides in the third game of the Division Series against the eventual champions.2 He leaves two years of a three-year, $75 million engagement on the table and collects a $5 million buyout for his trouble; San Diego holds the exclusive right to treat with him until Monday, and the two parties are reported still interested in a reunion. "San Diego has been incredible for me," the pitcher said upon the Friars' autumn exit. "I feel like I have a second home on the West Coast. It's been awesome. And I hope to continue it."2

Every club now does its winter sums, and none more gravely than the North Siders of Chicago, who watched the division rival they could not catch parade off with the whole pot. The Cubs could lose every one of the five men who finished the season in their rotation: Shota Imanaga, Kevin Gausman and David Peterson became free agents Thursday, Matthew Boyd and Clay Holmes are expected to join them by way of their option clauses, and Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki head the list of departing bats.3 The president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer, asked at his season's-end accounting why the gap to Milwaukee keeps widening, pointed at the champions' mound: "Their pitching has been exceptionally good. I think that's the area that we have to double down and really focus on."3

THE FIDELITY DESK: TWO MEN WEIGH THE OPEN ROAD AGAINST THE WARM HEARTH AND CHOOSE THE HEARTH — BICHETTE TAKES HIS TWO-AND-FORTY MILLIONS IN FLUSHING, HELSLEY HIS FOURTEEN IN BALTIMORE

Not every man with a door to the market walked through it. Bo Bichette has opted into the second season of his three-year, $126 million engagement, a source advises, and will reprise his role as the Metropolitans' third baseman at $42 million for 2027 — with the same escape clause waiting for him again next autumn. The first year in Queens was an uneven one: booed while going 1-for-14 across his first three home games, carrying an OPS below .600 as late as the 10th of June, then batting .285/.337/.442 the rest of the way — recovery enough for comfort, if not for the kind of winter that beats $84 million guaranteed. At 28 he has also grown into the role of tutor to the young men A.J. Ewing and Carson Benge, and by season's end professed himself considerably happier in the uniform than he began.4

In Baltimore, Ryan Helsley reached the same conclusion by a harder road. The right-hander is opting into his $14 million player option for 2027, a source confirms, after an injury-plagued season — a 4.11 earned-run average and eight saves in only 17 games, two stays in the infirmary for his elbow, and not a single appearance after the 27th of June, though the club expects him whole for the spring. The Birds' bullpen thus enters the winter holding both Helsley and the lately mended Félix Bautista, and the question of which man closes is now Baltimore's pleasant arithmetic to perform.5

THE OPTIONS LEDGER: ATLANTA SPENDS FOUR-AND-TWENTY MILLIONS TO KEEP ACUÑA AND ALBIES IN HARNESS, SEATTLE RETAINS ITS CLOSER, AND KANSAS CITY TURNS ITS OWN LOOSE

The day's heaviest traffic ran through the option clauses, where clubs across both leagues settled accounts. Atlanta exercised Ronald Acuña Jr.'s $17 million option and Ozzie Albies' $7 million one, keeping the old cornerstones side by side at least one season more. Acuña's year was the now-familiar mixture of brilliance and the trainer's table — .255 with 20 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a .796 OPS in 107 games, a third of the schedule lost to two separate hamstring strains, with a .997 OPS over his final 26 games to argue the talent remains. A further $17 million option for 2028 waits in his contract; Albies may test the market after 2027.6

In Seattle the Mariners exercised Andrés Muñoz's $9 million option despite the most trying season of his career — a 4.24 earned-run average and 10 blown saves, tying the most in the majors — while declining Bryce Miller's $6.075 million figure, though the right-hander remains under the club's control through arbitration to 2029. Victor Robles was let go to free agency, joining Randy Arozarena, J.P. Crawford, Hoby Milner and Taylor Ward among the Puget Sound men now free to sign anywhere beginning Monday afternoon.7 And in Kansas City the Royals declined their $13 million option on the closer Carlos Estévez — who led all baseball with 42 saves in 2025 and now takes a $2 million buyout to the open market — while exercising a $2.5 million option on the mending right-hander Tony Gonsolin, a 16-game winner for the 2022 Dodgers whom they will try in rotation or relief come spring.8

THE COMMERCE DESK: THE WINTER'S FIRST SWAP IS STRUCK BEFORE THE CHAMPAGNE IS MOPPED — THE WHITE ELEPHANTS FETCH THE UTILITY MAN EATON FROM THE HUB NINE FOR AN ARM OF EIGHTEEN SUMMERS

It wanted less than 24 hours after the final out for the first trade of the offseason to be struck. The Athletics on Thursday acquired the outfielder Nate Eaton from the Red Sox in exchange for the minor-league right-hander Jareth Rayo. Eaton, 29, caught in the crush of Boston's 40-man roster, batted a thin .160 in 24 games this season but carries a defender's résumé — all three outfield posts and third base besides — and gives the Athletics seasoned depth for the upper rungs of their system. Rayo, 18, signed out of Nicaragua in the 2024-25 international period, posted a 5.50 earned-run average with 36 strikeouts against 20 walks across 36 innings of the Dominican Summer League.9

The footnote is the front office. The swap is the first official act of Taylor Smith, the Athletics' newly installed president of baseball operations — and it was struck with the very Boston office he served under Craig Breslow from 2024 through this past season. The winter's dealings have begun with a man trading against his own former desk.9

THE PROCESSION DESK: MILWAUKEE SHUTS ITS SCHOOLHOUSES AND LINES WISCONSIN AVENUE THIS MORNING — THE CHAMPIONS SPENT THEIR EVE AT LAMBEAU FIELD, AND THE RELICS ARE ALREADY BOUND FOR COOPERSTOWN

The Parade of Champions, whose particulars this paper set down yesterday, steps off this very morning: 10 o'clock Central time, from North 4th Street and West Wisconsin Avenue, with the rally and fan festival to follow at Henry Maier Festival Park, all of it free to whoever arrives first. The city has cleared the way in the most literal sense — Milwaukee Public Schools closed every school and district office for the day, "due to operations and safety impacts from the Brewers parade and celebration," the official notice crowned with the words "Congrats World Champs."10

The champions rehearsed their celebrating Thursday night in Green Bay, where a cadre of Brewers — the veteran pitcher Brandon Woodruff striding at the front with the Commissioner's Trophy held high — crashed the Packers' game against the Panthers at Lambeau Field to a roar from the house. Sal Frelick, whose game-squaring home run turned the second game of the Series, could not resist the local sacrament: a picture-perfect Lambeau Leap into the first row beyond the end zone.11 And the museum men have already claimed their share of the October just closed. Bound for the Hall of Fame at Cooperstown: the chest protector and shin guards of the Series' most valuable player William Contreras, the manager Pat Murphy's postseason hooded sweatshirt, the unmistakable spectacles of the scoreless-innings man Aaron Ashby, and Frelick's batting gloves from that second game.12

A strange quiet this morning: for the first time since March, no contest stands behind this paper and none ahead of it. The schedule ledger has been consulted all the same, as it is every morning, and the page is white — 145 mornings of it, until Opening Night restores the game on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027, with the full slate following a day later.1 The Herald does not fold its tent for the cold months. The market opened within hours of the last out, as the columns above attest; the awards season and the winter's dealings lie ahead; and this paper will keep its daily watch over all of it, from the first opt-out to the last truck bound for the training camps. Today, though, belongs to Milwaukee, where the schoolhouses stand empty and Wisconsin Avenue fills. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: CHAMPIONS OF THE WORLD AT LAST — BREWERS 4, RAYS 1, THE SERIES IN FIVE, AND SEVEN-AND-FIFTY SEASONS OF WAITING END AT 11:13 UNDER THE TROPICANA ROOF
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 113 · Thursday, the Twenty-Ninth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

CHAMPIONS OF THE WORLD AT LAST — BREWERS 4, RAYS 1, THE SERIES IN FIVE, AND SEVEN-AND-FIFTY SEASONS OF WAITING END AT 11:13 UNDER THE TROPICANA ROOF

Misiorowski Scoreless Into the Sixth Until His Own Calf, Not a Ray, Removes Him; Pratt's Sixth Hit in Succession Breaks a 48-Year-Old Rookie Mark; Megill Gets the Groundout That Crowns Milwaukee; and 31,000 Fill the Ballpark Back Home to Watch a Scoreboard

The Milwaukee Brewers are champions of the world. The sentence has waited 57 seasons to be set in type — through the franchise's birth as the Seattle Pilots in 1969, through the seven-game heartbreak of 1982 in St. Louis, through eight Octobers entered in the last nine years and every one of them ended by another club's celebration — and it became true at 11:13 Wednesday night in St. Petersburg, 10:13 on the clocks of Wisconsin, when Richie Palacios chopped Trevor Megill's pitch to Brice Turang at second base and the throw beat him to the bag. Brewers 4, Rays 1; the Series, four games to one. Back home, 31,000 had filled American Family Field to watch on the scoreboard a game played 1,200 miles away, and what they saw was the city's first baseball championship since the Braves' of 1957 — won in the 44th year since Milwaukee last reached a Series, by a club that plays beneath Henry Aaron's retired No. 44.3

A day after Tampa Bay tore the championship page out of the book in the twelfth inning — the reprieve these columns chronicled yesterday — Milwaukee simply wrote it over again, this time in ink. Jacob Misiorowski, handed the assignment yesterday's paper called the best arm in the game, was exactly that: 5 2/3 scoreless innings on two hits, 51 of his pitches arriving at 100 miles an hour or better, until a cramping calf — no Tampa bat managed it — removed him in the sixth.35 The rookie Cooper Pratt singled home Turang in the second for a fifth consecutive hit, then singled again in the fifth for a sixth — breaking Brian Doyle's 48-year-old record for a rookie in a World's Series, making him the first man of any tenure with six straight Series hits since David Ortiz in 2013, and leaving him one shy of Billy Hatcher's all-time seven — and came around on David Hamilton's knock moments later.65 William Contreras doubled home Christian Yelich in the sixth, Pratt's sacrifice fly made it 4-0, and the evening's remaining suspense concerned only the champagne. Drew Rasmussen, who took the ball on three days' rest after all despite his club's stated reluctance, gave four honest innings and was charged with the loss; six relievers followed him.9

Tampa Bay's lone answer came in the ninth, when Liam Hicks' double struck first base and caromed away crazily and Chandler Simpson doubled him home. Megill allowed the run and nothing more, got his groundout, and threw his fists at the tilted white roof.3 The record-keepers will want a week with this club. Milwaukee finished its October 11 wins against 2 defeats, only the fifth club ever to win eleven postseason games while losing two or fewer; it allowed more than four runs in none of its thirteen contests, a thing done by a champion previously only by the 1983 Orioles and the 1990 Reds; and it welded that October to a franchise-record 103-win season, the best in the game.53

Then came the scenes a city rehearses for 57 years. Yelich, the captain, who arrived in 2018 and stayed for this: "I blacked out on the field as soon as I saw 'Rang throw it over to first base. I don't remember what happened. I think I ran to Megill first. What a feeling." Robin Yount, who wore Milwaukee's colors in the 1982 defeat, sought out the 22-year-old Pratt amid the delirium to tell him, "You're one heck of a shortstop." And the manager Pat Murphy, 67 years old and lately acquainted with every variety of October grief, put the season's epitaph plainly: "We came in with a spirit about us, and we weren't going to be denied."36

News Around the League

THE LAURELS DESK: CONTRERAS, MASTER OF THE NEW CHALLENGE SYSTEM AND WARDEN OF THE RUNNING GAME, TAKES THE WILLIE MAYS TROPHY — THE FIRST CATCHER SO HONORED SINCE 2015, AND A CHAMPION TWICE IN A SINGLE YEAR

The Most Valuable Player of this World's Series is its catcher. William Contreras, 28, stood at the center of the podium with the Willie Mays trophy aloft, having gone 8-for-21 with four runs batted in — among them the sixth-inning double that scored Yelich with the insurance run of the clinching game — while his pitchers compiled a 1.91 earned-run average and held Tampa Bay to a .182 figure for the five games. He is the eighth catcher to take the Series' highest individual honor and the first since Salvador Perez in 2015.4

The work behind the plate was the argument. The Rays arrived having stolen eleven bases in eleven October attempts; Contreras threw out four of the nine men who dared him. And in the first season of the automated ball-strike challenge system at the game's highest level, he proved its first October master: 10 of his 13 challenges in the Series were overturned in Milwaukee's favor, against a regular-season rate of 60 percent for fielders, and 67 percent across his 33 challenges this postseason. "How he does the ABS thing, I don't know," said Murphy, "but the guy has a knack for it."4 The year now closes in a perfect ring: Contreras, Jackson Chourio and Antonio Senzatela, champions with Venezuela in the spring's World Baseball Classic, become only the second set of teammates to win that tournament and the World's Series in the same year, after Alex Bregman and Luke Gregerson in 2017 — and William joins his brother Willson, champion with the 2016 Cubs, in the tenth brotherhood ever to put a World's Series ring on each hand.5

THE RECORD-BOOK DESK: THE FOURTH-LONGEST WAIT FOR A FIRST TITLE ENDS IN A FORTNIGHT OF DEMOLITION — A BULLPEN AT 1.38, ASHBY'S EIGHTEEN SPOTLESS INNINGS BESIDE WHITEY FORD, AND TWO BOYS OF TWO-AND-TWENTY WITH EIGHT HITS APIECE

The ledger of this championship will be consulted for decades, so the Herald sets down its principal entries now. The 57 seasons Milwaukee waited for a first title are the fourth-longest such vigil ever kept — the Phillies waited 77, the Browns-turned-Orioles 63, the Senators-turned-Rangers 62.5 The pitching carried it: Milwaukee's relief corps worked 65 of the staff's 118 October innings and answered with a 1.38 earned-run average and a .173 opponents' mark, each figure the second-stingiest any bullpen has posted in a postseason.5

Chief among those arms stands Aaron Ashby, whose spotless streak these columns have followed since he passed Gossage a week ago Sunday. The final accounting: 18 innings this October, every one scoreless, tying Whitey Ford's 1960 for the third-most all-scoreless innings in any single postseason, behind only Christy Mathewson's 27 of 1905 and Kenny Rogers' 23 of 2006 — and no other pitcher in playoff history has recorded five or more outs in seven consecutive scoreless appearances. He permitted five hits all month, walked three, struck out twenty, and watched the final out from the bullpen with a ball in his glove, ready for an inning that never came.57 The youth movement wrote its own pages: Chourio and Pratt, each 22, became the first teammates so young to collect eight hits apiece in the same postseason series; Chourio's 11 hits in the five games trail only Pepper Martin's 12 of 1931 through a Series' first five; and Pratt's seven runs batted in tied Gil McDougald's 1951 mark for a rookie, his final line reading .421 with two doubles, a home run, and one ovation from Robin Yount.56

THE CIVIC DESK: MILWAUKEE DECLARES FRIDAY A DAY OF PROCESSION — THE PARADE OF CHAMPIONS STEPS OFF AT TEN O'CLOCK FROM FOURTH AND WISCONSIN, WITH A RALLY AT THE LAKEFRONT AND A SHOWING OF "UECK" TO FOLLOW

The trophy travels north, and the city has fixed the hour of its welcome. The Brewers' Parade of Champions steps off Friday at 10 o'clock in the morning, Central time, from North 4th Street and West Wisconsin Avenue in downtown Milwaukee, concluding with a rally and fan festival at Henry Maier Festival Park on the lakefront. Admission asks nothing but promptness: the whole affair is free and open to the public, first come, first served.8

The rally's program carries one entry that will wet more eyes than the champagne did: alongside the alumni, the live music and a commemorative rally towel, the club will offer a special showing of Ueck, the documentary on the late Bob Uecker, fifty years the voice of this franchise, who died in January of 2025 with the drought still standing. The parade he never got to call now rolls, in part, for him.8

THE REQUIEM DESK: THREE JOURNEYS TO THE WORLD'S SERIES AND THREE EMPTY-HANDED RETURNS — THE RAYS, PICKED LAST IN THEIR DIVISION IN THE SPRING, LEAVE THE FIELD IN TEARS AND IN CREDIT BOTH

The visiting clubhouse's joy had its mirror down the corridor. Tampa Bay, picked by the wise men of the spring to finish last in its own division, instead spent most of the summer with the American League's best record, took the East from the Yankees in their own ballpark, swept those same Yankees out of October, and won the pennant under a roof that a hurricane had torn off two years before — and then met a better club. It is the franchise's third World's Series and its third defeat, after 2008 and 2020, and the Rays remain one of four clubs never to win the last game of a season, alongside the Padres, Mariners and Rockies — a list the Brewers departed Wednesday night.9

"I'm crushed right now, disappointed," said the manager Kevin Cash. "But it's easier to handle because of what we all meant to each other throughout the course of this season." Junior Caminero, true to the vow this paper printed yesterday, played on his wounded foot and singled once. Jonathan Aranda, the longest-tenured man in the organization, stood before his locker more than an hour after the final out, still in full uniform, the Series patch on his shoulder, while his teammates dressed and went home around him. The last word belongs to Drew Rasmussen, who started the clincher on short rest and lost it: "You just don't know how many opportunities you're going to get, especially in this game. So, to be this close, it really hurts."9

So ends the 2026 baseball year: 113 editions of this paper from the first pitch of spring to the last out of October, and the final score of the final game reads Brewers 4, Rays 1. The schedule ledger has been consulted this morning as it is every morning, and it stands empty — no contest today, none tomorrow, none until Opening Night brings the game back on March 24 of 2027, with the full card following a day later.2 What remains is ceremony and ledger-keeping: the parade up Wisconsin Avenue on Friday morning,8 and then the long winter of awards, auctions and argument, through which the Herald will publish as faithfully as ever. One image to carry into it: through this whole season, the Brewers' clubhouse manager Tony Migliaccio, a batboy with the club in 1978, kept in his pocket a coin struck by Judy Uecker after her husband's death — Bob's face on one side, and on the other his final sign-off on the Brewers' radio wire: So long, everybody!3 The old announcer's team are champions of the world, and this paper can think of no better words to close an October on. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: THREE OUTS FROM THE FIRST TITLE IN MILWAUKEE'S HISTORY, AND TAMPA BAY TEARS THE PAGE OUT — RAYS 4, BREWERS 3 IN THE TWELFTH, AND THE BROOM GOES BACK IN THE CLOSET
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 112 · Wednesday, the Twenty-Eighth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THREE OUTS FROM THE FIRST TITLE IN MILWAUKEE'S HISTORY, AND TAMPA BAY TEARS THE PAGE OUT — RAYS 4, BREWERS 3 IN THE TWELFTH, AND THE BROOM GOES BACK IN THE CLOSET

Pratt's Fourth Hit Is a Homer That Stands Half an Inning as the Championship Stroke; a Bounced Throw, Four Singles and the Season Is Saved; Ashby Runs His Spotless October to Eighteen Innings and Past Andrew Miller's Mark; Only the 1910 Cubs Ever Won in the Last At-Bat With a Sweep Overhead

Milwaukee stood three outs from the first championship in its history, and the man who had seemingly delivered it was a rookie of 22. Cooper Pratt — whose error-and-atonement these columns chronicled Sunday — led off the twelfth against Ian Seymour with his fourth hit of the night, a drive into the left-center seats that broke a tie standing since the fifth inning. His final line read 4-for-5 with a double besides, the finest evening of his young October life. Half an inning later the blow was a footnote.

The unmaking began, as so much of this Series has, with a throw. Joey Ortiz fielded Junior Caminero's leadoff grounder at third and bounced his long peg off Jake Bauers' glove, and the Rays' third baseman was aboard — limping, of which more below. Shane Drohan, a rookie left-hander summoned from the bullpen, never recorded an out: Liam Hicks ground a single through the left side, Caminero hobbling to third; Jonny DeLuca's single up the middle scored Cedric Mullins, running for the wounded man, to square it; Chandler Simpson's third hit of the night filled the bases; and Ben Williamson, sent up to pinch-hit, chopped a bounder into right field to score Nick Fortes with the run that ended it — 4-3, after four hours and twenty minutes, before 40,514 under the closed roof. "We pieced together a big inning," said the Tampa Bay manager Kevin Cash, "maybe the most important inning of our season."3

The eleven innings before had been the tight, low-scoring kind this Series keeps producing. Simpson doubled home DeLuca in the second; Pratt doubled home Sal Frelick in the fourth; Caminero crossed with the lead that same frame when David Hamilton missed a tag and threw wild; Hamilton atoned in the fifth with a fly over the right-center barrier, and there the score sat, 2-2, for seven innings of fine margins — Brice Turang turning two on a 101.8-mph line drive off Jonathan Aranda's bat, Simpson going up the left-field wall to rob Garrett Mitchell, Pratt ruled out on review stealing second in the ninth.3 And Aaron Ashby, arriving in the ninth of a tie game, retired all seven men he faced. His spotless October now runs to eighteen innings, past Andrew Miller's sixteen of 2016 for the longest by a relief man in any single postseason by the Elias Bureau's accounting — a march these columns have followed since he passed Gossage on Sunday.5

The record books required attention when it was over. Tampa Bay is the 44th club to fall three games behind in a best-of-seven and only the eleventh to dodge the sweep — the fifth to force a fifth game of a World's Series, after the 1910 Cubs, 1937 Giants, 1970 Reds and 2024 Yankees, and not one of those four ever forced a sixth. It was the seventeenth time a club facing elimination won a Series game in its last at-bat, the first since the 2011 Cardinals turned the trick on this very calendar date, and the 1910 Cubs remain the only other club to manage it with a sweep hanging overhead.4 Milwaukee's run of eight October victories in succession, whose record-tying length these columns noted only yesterday, ends at eight. "We've got one more day," said Seymour, who surrendered Pratt's homer and won the game anyway. The arithmetic still leans hard toward Wisconsin — three games to one, the best arm in baseball waiting tonight — but there has been no sweep of a World's Series since 2012, fourteen Octobers running, and this one has now joined the streak.4

News Around the League

THE ASSIGNMENT DESK: MILWAUKEE SENDS THE BEST ARM IN THE LEAGUE TO FINISH THE BUSINESS — MISIOROWSKI AND HIS 1.80 TONIGHT, WHILE TAMPA BAY, ITS STARTERS ALL SPENT, PREPARES A NIGHT OF COMMITTEE WORK

The fifth game belongs to Jacob Misiorowski, and the Cream City nine could ask for no better custodian. The right-hander led all baseball this season in earned-run average (1.80), strikeouts (252), WHIP (0.80) and opponents' batting average (.157), and his October has kept the pattern: three starts, a 2.70 average, and one run on four hits across five innings in the opening game of this Series. He takes the hill tonight on his full four days of rest.6

Tampa Bay, by contrast, opens the cupboard and finds it nearly bare. Five of its starters have pitched within the past four games; Drew Rasmussen is held unlikely to return on three days' rest; and Nick Martinez, who had been expected to start tonight, instead spent two scoreless innings keeping the twelfth-inning miracle possible.3 The likeliest course is a bullpen night — Cole Sulser, Steven Matz and Garrett Cleavinger, none of whom pitched Tuesday, are the freshest men in the house, while the closer Bryan Baker worked two innings and 21 pitches, his first such outing since 2024. The consolation of survival: should the Tampa men steal tonight's game, Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta stand rested and lined up for the sixth and seventh.6

THE INFIRMARY DESK: CAMINERO LIMPS THROUGH THE WINNING RALLY AND VOWS TO PLAY ON A BROKEN FOOT IF HE MUST — WHILE McCLANAHAN'S FOREARM CLOSES HIS OCTOBER FOR GOOD

Junior Caminero came up lame after reaching on Ortiz's twelfth-inning error, gimped from first to third on Hicks' single anyway, and yielded to a pinch-runner — and he does not propose to let any of it matter. "If my foot is broken," the 23-year-old third baseman said afterward, "I'll play tomorrow." He would not reveal the extent of the injury to his left foot. His manager settled the question from the other direction: "He'll play tomorrow on one leg. I'll make sure of it," said Kevin Cash, whose club is batting .195 with a single home run in this Series and can ill spare the man who hit 42 homers with 101 runs batted in while playing all 162 games this season — even an October version of him who has managed one homer and five runs batted in across 13 games.7

The same ward carries a harder verdict. Shane McClanahan, the Rays' oft-mended left-hander, has been ruled out for the remainder of the postseason with tightness in his forearm; the club expects him ready by spring. The spring is small comfort to a team whose season now lives one night at a time.6

THE INSTRUCTION DESK: THE FATSE ENGAGEMENT IS MADE OFFICIAL — PHILADELPHIA SEATS ITS NEW PROFESSOR OF HITTING, ADDS CRONIN TO THE FACULTY, AND KEEPS GONZALEZ ON STAFF

The hiring this paper reported yesterday on the word of a source is now official: the Phillies on Tuesday announced Peter Fatse as their hitting coach. "I am very excited to add Pete to our staff," said the manager Don Mattingly in the club's statement. "He has a track record of being a great communicator who prioritizes collaboration." The club also engaged Joe Cronin — six years in the Boston organization, lately a hitting-strategy man on its big-league staff — as an assistant hitting coach, and retained Edwar Gonzalez in the same capacity.8

The commission is as yesterday's columns described it: succeed Kevin Long, and raise an offense that slid from eighth in baseball in runs in 2025 (778) to nineteenth (713) this past season.8

THE STEWARDSHIP DESK: BALTIMORE'S NEW GENERAL MANAGER MEETS THE PRESS AND THE FRUSTRATION BOTH — BANNER, LATELY OF THE CUBS' FRONT OFFICE, PROMISES A WINNER AND PRACTICES THAT FEEL LIKE GAMES

The Orioles introduced Jared Banner as their general manager Tuesday, and the new man began by acknowledging the ledger. "To the fans, I want you to know: I know you're frustrated. It's been a rough couple of years," he told his introductory news conference. "We're frustrated too. But you have our commitment. We're going to build a winner here in Baltimore." Banner arrives from the Cubs, where he was an assistant general manager, and inherits a club that won the American League East in 2023, took a wild card in 2024, and has since posted two losing seasons running while its young cornerstones — Gunnar Henderson, Colton Cowser, Jackson Holliday — went backward.9

The division of labor is explicit. Mike Elias, elevated to the club presidency last year, keeps scouting and acquisition — professional, international, amateur, the contracts — while Banner takes everything internal: player development, performance, health, the coaching ranks. The new man's stated philosophy is a workman's one. "We have to make practice more like the game, so the game gets easier once you get in there," he said, promising to "challenge all of our processes" and to "get comfortable being uncomfortable."9

THE OLD GUARD DESK: POSADA, SEVENTEEN YEARS A YANKEE AND NEVER ANYTHING ELSE, SAYS HE NO LONGER FEELS WANTED IN THE BRONX — AND PRESCRIBES A STERNER VOICE FOR THE CLUBHOUSE HE LEFT

Jorge Posada says he stays away from the ballpark he helped fill because he no longer feels asked. "I mean, I could, but I don't think they want me there, to tell you the truth," the old catcher said in an interview on the New York Post's podcast The Show, published Tuesday. "I don't feel welcome when I go there, you know? ... I don't feel like they want me there, so I don't go." He traced part of the estrangement to his final season of 2011, when he was moved off the catching position and quarreled with the management over playing time: "It's tough to go back and feel that again."10

The grievance came wrapped in a prescription. Posada, a five-time champion, urged the Yankees to install a voice that holds men to account in June so the bill does not come due in October: "You didn't run to first base? Get him out of the game. ... It's not a game, it's really a job, and some guys are not doing their job." He was careful, even so, to endorse the stewardship of Brian Cashman and Aaron Boone as the right men for the leading of it.10

The Series stands three games to one, and the road ahead has been checked against the schedule ledger: the fifth game tonight at eight o'clock Eastern under the Tropicana roof, and then — should Tampa Bay keep the argument alive — a sixth in Milwaukee on Friday the 30th and a seventh on Saturday the 31st, All Hallows' Eve.2 The sum is simple. The Rays must now take three in a row from a club that needs one win in three tries, two of those tries at home with the best record in its league behind them; the one rope out of this hole, as this paper wrote yesterday, has been climbed to the top exactly once, by the 2004 Red Sox. But last night the 44th club to grab that rope gained a handhold, and tonight it sends a wounded third baseman and a patchwork pitching staff against the finest arm in the game, with nothing at stake except whether anyone in Wisconsin sleeps before Friday. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: SEVEN HITS IN SUCCESSION, EIGHT RUNS AFTER TWO WERE DOWN — BREWERS 10, RAYS 1, AND MILWAUKEE STANDS ONE WIN FROM THE FIRST CHAMPIONSHIP IN ITS HISTORY
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 111 · Tuesday, the Twenty-Seventh of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

SEVEN HITS IN SUCCESSION, EIGHT RUNS AFTER TWO WERE DOWN — BREWERS 10, RAYS 1, AND MILWAUKEE STANDS ONE WIN FROM THE FIRST CHAMPIONSHIP IN ITS HISTORY

Gasser Honors the Family Name With Six Spotless Innings on a Single Hit; the Fifth Inning Does Two Things No World's Series Inning Ever Did; Chourio's Four Knocks Are the Youngest Man's Since 1946; and Woodruff, Silent Since the Fourth of July, Throws the Final Pitch Before 40,388

The new roof at Tropicana Field, whose restoration this paper saluted only yesterday, proved weatherproof Monday night but not Milwaukee-proof. The third game of the World's Series ended 10-1, the Series stands three games to none, and the visiting clubhouse now sits one victory from the first championship the Milwaukee franchise has ever possessed. The early innings gave no hint of the avalanche. Robert Gasser — whose father's forty-year-old draft story ran in these columns yesterday morning — honored the patrimony with six innings of one-hit, scoreless pitching, walking one and striking out three, while his mates built a modest lead in the third: Christian Yelich lining a single to left to score Jackson Chourio, Jake Bauers coming across on William Contreras' knock to right, the catcher thrown out stretching for second on Victor Mesa Jr.'s throw. Two runs after four innings, and a tidy evening in prospect.

Then came the fifth, and the record book required two new pages. Twelve Milwaukee men batted; eight of them hit safely, seven in unbroken succession — a thing no club had done in any World's Series game — and every one of the eight runs scored after two were out, a sum no Series inning had ever yielded from that position.3 The inning turned on Yelich's legs and a camera: ruled forced at second on a grounder, he was reprieved on Milwaukee's challenge, and the procession resumed.3 Brice Turang singled home two, Garrett Mitchell singled home another, the rookie Cooper Pratt doubled home two more, Sal Frelick doubled, David Hamilton singled, and Chourio capped the carnage with a double of his own — 10-0 before the Gulf Coast club had managed a third hit. Freddy Peralta, whose homecoming form this paper had carried as Tampa Bay's best remaining argument, was charged with five runs in 4 2/3 innings, and Cam Booser faced four men without retiring one.

Chourio's evening deserves its own ledger line: 4-for-5 with a stolen base, and at 22 years and 229 days the youngest man to collect four hits in a World's Series game since Joe Garagiola in 1946 — one short of the single-game record held by Paul Molitor, of the 1982 Brewers, and Albert Pujols.4 Through three games the leadoff man is batting .571, with eight hits and three stolen bases.4

The coda belonged to an older arm. Brandon Woodruff, whose twice-repaired shoulder had not thrown a competitive pitch since July 4 — a vigil this paper has kept since the roster was set — walked to the mound for the ninth, allowed a run on Cedric Mullins' swinging bunt and Yandy Díaz's double, and recorded the final out of a 10-1 night.5 The win ran Milwaukee's streak to eight postseason victories in succession, tying the longest any club has strung together within a single October; of the 43 clubs that ever led a best-of-seven series three games to none, 42 finished the work.3 The fourth game goes tonight at eight o'clock Eastern, under the same roof.

News Around the League

THE BRINK DESK: TWO-AND-FORTY OF THREE-AND-FORTY CLUBS UP THREE GAMES TO NONE HAVE FINISHED THE BUSINESS — TONIGHT JAX TAKES THE BALL FOR TAMPA BAY, MILWAUKEE NAMES NO MAN AT ALL, AND HISTORY OFFERS THE RAYS EXACTLY ONE ROPE

The assignment this paper anticipated Monday has come to pass: Kevin Cash, having held Griffin Jax out of the third game, hands his right-hander the ball tonight with the season in the balance. The form is genuine — a 1.88 earned-run average across 24 innings over his last six outings — and this will be only his third appearance of the postseason, so the arm is fresh for whatever length the evening demands.6

Milwaukee, for its part, has named nobody. Woodruff had been the presumptive man for the fourth game before his ninth-inning turn Monday, and the club's remaining options are the right-hander Dustin May, the left-handers Kyle Harrison and Shane Drohan, or a reliever sent out to open.6 A club up three games to none can afford improvisation; a club down three games to none cannot afford anything else. The one rope history offers Tampa Bay is the 2004 Red Sox, the only club ever to climb out of that hole in postseason play — and Milwaukee has its own page in prospect, for no club has swept both the pennant round and the World's Series since the former lengthened to seven games in 1985.3 Eight o'clock Eastern, the Tropicana roof, the FOX wire.

THE CLEMENTE DESK: BEFORE THE THIRD GAME THE COMMISSIONER HANDED LINDOR THE GAME'S HIGHEST OFF-FIELD HONOR — THE FIFTH SON OF PUERTO RICO TO RECEIVE IT

The evening's one ceremony preceded its demolition. On the field at Tropicana Field before Monday's game, the commissioner Rob Manfred presented Francisco Lindor, shortstop of the New York Mets, with the league's Roberto Clemente Award for 2026 — the honor conferred each year upon the player whose philanthropy best carries the great Pittsburgh outfielder's example — with Lindor's wife, parents and family in attendance.7 He is the fifth Puerto Rican player so honored, following Edgar Martínez, Carlos Delgado, Carlos Beltrán and Yadier Molina.7

The citation is earned in brick and tuition as much as in sentiment. Since 2020 Lindor has given more than a million dollars toward Lindor Hall, a middle-school building at his old academy at Montverde, Florida, with a scholarship fund attached for students who could not otherwise attend; after the hurricanes Maria and Fiona he funded relief and restored athletic grounds in his native Caguas; and his season-long program of mentorship in Queens attends to the minds of young athletes as carefully as their bodies.7 The Herald, which spends its October columns on men who hit baseballs, is glad once a year to salute a man for what he builds.

THE INSTRUCTION DESK: PHILADELPHIA ENGAGES A NEW PROFESSOR OF HITTING — FATSE, LATELY OF BOSTON, TO SUCCEED KEVIN LONG, BY A REPORT THE CLUB HAS YET TO CONFIRM

The Phillies have engaged Peter Fatse as their new hitting coach, by the account of a source — the hiring first reported by The Athletic, and not yet confirmed by the club itself — to succeed Kevin Long after an offense that ranked eighth in baseball in runs in 2025 slipped to nineteenth this season.8

Fatse arrives with a resume of both ascent and abrupt ending: assistant hitting coach in Boston for two seasons, then the Red Sox's lead hitting man from December 2021 until April of this past season, when he was let go in the same stroke that claimed the manager Alex Cora. Before Boston he coordinated the Twins' minor-league hitting, and before any of it the Brewers drafted him in the 24th round of 2009 — a playing career of two minor-league seasons that turned him early to the teaching trade.8

THE VACANCY DESK: SEATTLE'S SEARCH NARROWS TO AN OLD HAND AND A NEW ONE — ESPADA AND KANZLER SIT FOR THIRD INTERVIEWS WHILE THE REPORTED FRONTRUNNER WITHDRAWS FOR FAMILY'S SAKE

The Mariners, a month without a manager since parting with Dan Wilson at the season's end, have brought two candidates to the ballpark in person: Joe Espada, 51, three seasons the manager in Houston and six a bench coach there before that, and Jason Kanzler, 36, the Cubs' director of player development, who has run that farm system for three seasons and has never managed at any level. For both men it is a third round of interviews, the earlier two conducted by wire.9

The field has thinned around them. Rocco Baldelli, reported the frontrunner, withdrew for family reasons — his people are settled in Florida, and Seattle is a long way from there — a departure first reported by Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic and confirmed to MLB.com by a source. Walker McKinven of the White Sox was interviewed and is reported out of the running; the president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto has set no timetable, and has said previous managing experience is preferred but not required — a standard his last two hires, Scott Servais and Wilson himself, did not meet either.9

THE FACULTY DESK: MARIANO DUNCAN, FIVE YEARS THE BENCH COACH AT BINGHAMTON, ASCENDS TO THE METROPOLITAN STAFF — A NEWLY MADE POST, BY THE ACCOUNT OF A PERSON FAMILIAR WITH THE PLANS

The Mets are promoting Mariano Duncan to a newly created Major League coaching post, by the account of a person familiar with the plans — the club has not yet confirmed it — in which he will work with the position players across several departments and throw batting practice besides. Duncan has spent eight years in the organization, the last five as bench coach at Double-A Binghamton, where the likes of Francisco Alvarez and Brett Baty passed through his schoolroom on their way to Queens; a temporary big-league assignment after the Double-A season has now been made permanent.10

The new professor's own credentials were earned in October. As a player Duncan won the World's Series with the 1990 Reds and again with the 1996 Yankees, and took a pennant besides with the 1993 Phillies — a man who knows the view from both ends of a champagne celebration, now charged with teaching the route.10

Three games to none, and Milwaukee has now won eight postseason games in succession — a streak that has tied the longest ever assembled within a single October, with sole possession of the record on offer tonight.3 The particulars ahead are verified and as follows: the fourth game this evening at eight o'clock Eastern under the Tropicana roof, the fifth there Wednesday should the question survive the night, and the Series returning to Milwaukee for Friday the 30th and — at the uttermost — Saturday the 31st, All Hallows' Eve.2 The Rays must now win four games in succession from a club that has won its last eight, a feat accomplished exactly once in the history of postseason play; the Brewers need win only one, and have four chances to do it. Forty-four years ago Milwaukee came to a World's Series and left empty-handed. Tonight the city could put the matter right by bedtime. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Postseason Off-Day Edition — the Twenty-Sixth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 110 · Monday, the Twenty-Sixth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the pennant races rest.

0 days until the third game of the 122nd World's Series — Gasser against Peralta under the Tropicana roof, eight o'clock this very evening (Monday, the 26th of October, 2026).

News Around the League

THE RESUMPTION DESK: AN IDLE SUNDAY SPENT AT ALTITUDE, AND THE ARGUMENT RECONVENES TONIGHT UNDER THE ST. PETERSBURG DOME — OF THE SEVEN-AND-FIFTY CLUBS THAT EVER LED A SERIES TWO GAMES TO NONE, SIX-AND-FORTY FINISHED THE BUSINESS

No baseball was played yesterday, and none was missed: Sunday belonged to the airlines, the Brewers flying south under family colors (as this paper reported) and the Rays returning home to reckon what went wrong in Milwaukee. The reckoning resumes tonight at eight o'clock Eastern at Tropicana Field, and the arithmetic the Rays carry into it is unfriendly. Of the 57 clubs that ever took a World's Series lead of two games to none, 46 went on to take the championship3 — though the optimists of Tampa Bay may answer that 16 clubs have climbed out of that very hole6, and that both of Milwaukee's wins were had by a single run.

The pitching assignment is the one this paper set out Sunday: Freddy Peralta, the exile, against the club that raised him — and opposite him Robert Gasser, Milwaukee's left-hander, whose own story is told below. Peralta's late-season ledger remains the best argument the Rays have: 7-0 with a 0.89 earned-run average over his last ten appearances, and a 1.45 mark in seven starts under his home roof since the July trade that brought him.3 Gasser answers with 2-0 and a 1.51 figure across eight appearances since late August, and a single run allowed in nine October innings.3

One Milwaukee footnote persists: Brandon Woodruff, whose 50-50 case this paper followed onto the roster on Friday, has yet to throw a pitch in the Series — his last appearance in any game remains July 4.3

THE ROOF DESK: THE HURRICANE TORE IT OFF, THE CITY PAID TO PUT IT BACK — AFTER EIGHTEEN YEARS THE WORLD'S SERIES RETURNS TO TROPICANA FIELD, A BALLPARK LATELY REBUILT AND LATELY FULL

Tonight's game is the first World's Series baseball played at Tropicana Field since 2008, and that the building stands ready to receive it is a civic feat worth a paragraph of its own. In the fall of 2024 the hurricane Milton tore the roof clean off the dome. The city of St. Petersburg, bound by contract to repair what the storm had wrecked, voted nearly 60 million dollars to the work — over the doubts of the club's own leadership, who questioned whether it could be done at that price or in time — and baseball returned under the new roof on April 6 of this year.4 The mayor, Ken Welch, calls the building "a great symbol of resilience"; the club's chief executive, Ken Babby, pronounced it "a great American comeback story" when the gates reopened.4

The comeback has found its audience. The Rays have opened the upper deck for October and drawn an average of 37,697 across five postseason dates, winning four of the five4 — and the house records one debt still outstanding: in the only other Series the building ever held, Tampa Bay won but a single home game, the second of the 2008 set against Philadelphia.4 The tenants would consider three wins in three nights a handsome way to square the account.

THE PATRIMONY DESK: MILWAUKEE DRAFTED A GASSER IN 1984 AND NEVER GOT HIM TO A MOUND — TWO-AND-FORTY YEARS LATER HIS SON TAKES THE BALL FOR THE SAME CLUB IN THE WORLD'S SERIES

The Brewers drafted a Gasser once before. In 1984 they selected Jim Gasser, a hitter by trade whom the club proposed to convert to pitching; he never threw for them, was drafted again by the Giants in 1986, and an elbow injury closed the book before a professional chapter could be written.5 Tonight, 42 years after Milwaukee first called the family name, his son Robert starts the third game of the World's Series for that same club.

The son's road this season was its own trial: left off the Opening Day roster, sent down to Nashville with a balky arm and no feel for his pitches, and recalled only after the feel returned. It has returned emphatically. His two October starts came in the enemy's parks at San Diego and Los Angeles, and across those nine innings he has surrendered one run — a Fernando Tatis Jr. home run — and nothing else.5

Gasser's parents will be in the seats tonight, stationed by agreement at a prudent remove from the bullpen rail, having found the proximity of earlier rounds hard on the nerves. His scouting report on himself: "I wasn't sure I was going to survive the LCS."5

THE SALVAGE DESK: PLAY CLEAN, BUILD A BRIDGE, AND REMEMBER CLEVELAND — THE RAYS' PRESCRIPTION FOR CLIMBING OUT OF A TWO-GAME HOLE

The Rays spent the idle day writing prescriptions, and the first is the simplest. "We've got to play clean versus those guys," said the left fielder Chandler Simpson6 — an echo of the sermon Junior Caminero delivered on his feet in the Game 2 dugout, which this paper recorded yesterday. The club that beat itself least from April to September has beaten itself twice in October, and knows it.

The second prescription concerns the middle innings. The ends of the bullpen are sound — Bryan Baker closing, Cam Booser from the left side — but the bridge between starter and finisher has leaked badly: Kevin Kelly has allowed eight hits in four October innings, Tyler Wells stands charged with five runs on six hits, and Ian Seymour threw the pitch Sal Frelick carried to dead center Saturday.6 Unless Peralta works deep tonight, somebody in that middle company must become dependable. The manager Kevin Cash may hold Griffin Jax back to start or carry the bulk of Game 4, which would line up Nick Martinez, Drew Rasmussen and Peralta again for whatever games follow6 — a plan drawn without Shane McClanahan, lost to the postseason with forearm tightness.3

The third prescription is memory. These same Rays trailed Cleveland two games to one in the league series and won it6; the hole is deeper now, but the shovel is familiar.

THE HAGGLER'S DESK: A BOY OF EIGHTEEN ASKS WHETHER A MILLION DOLLARS SHOULD STAND BETWEEN THE BREWERS AND A HALL OF FAMER — THE CLUB PAID UP, THE MAN NOW DENIES SAYING IT, AND EIGHT YEARS ON THE LEDGER LEANS HIS WAY

Every World's Series surfaces an origin story, and Milwaukee's second baseman owns the best-disputed one of this edition. In 2018 the Brewers drafted Brice Turang 21st overall out of Santiago High School in Corona, California, and the two sides haggled over the signing bonus with the boy holding a scholarship to Louisiana State as his leverage. By the account Bob Nightengale published in USA Today last May, Turang asked the general manager David Stearns whether the club would truly let a million dollars stand between it and a Hall of Famer.7

Here the testimony divides. Matt Arnold, then on the call and now president of the club's baseball operations, swears he heard the line. Turang remembers asking about the college money and nothing grander — and when Arnold suggested the agent had fed his client the flourish, Turang denied that too: "I never said that, either!"7

Whatever was said, the investment has matured. Turang's batting line has climbed from a .585 OPS in 2023 to .816 this season, with 21 home runs and 100 runs batted in; he took home both the Gold Glove and the National League's Platinum Glove in 2024 and is a finalist again.7 The Hall of Fame withholds judgment, as is its custom, but the haggler has long since covered the million.

A day of rest in October is a contradiction the calendar insists upon, and yesterday was one: no pitch thrown, no run scored, the whole argument suspended at two games to none while the principals changed addresses. Tonight it resumes indoors in Florida, and the particulars ahead are verified and as follows: the third, fourth and fifth games at Tropicana Field tonight, Tuesday and Wednesday, the Series returning to Milwaukee on Friday should a sixth game be required, and the seventh — should the argument run its full length — falling on Saturday, the 31st of October, All Hallows' Eve.2 The Rays need win only enough to get the trunks repacked; the Brewers, two wins from the first championship in the whole of their franchise's history, would prefer the luggage stay where it is.3 Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THE BOY OF TWO-AND-TWENTY WHO LET THE RAYS IN SHOWS THEM OUT — BREWERS 5, RAYS 4, A FOUR-RUN DEBT PAID IN FULL, AND MILWAUKEE REMOVES SOUTH TWO GAMES TO THE GOOD
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 109 · Sunday, the Twenty-Fifth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE BOY OF TWO-AND-TWENTY WHO LET THE RAYS IN SHOWS THEM OUT — BREWERS 5, RAYS 4, A FOUR-RUN DEBT PAID IN FULL, AND MILWAUKEE REMOVES SOUTH TWO GAMES TO THE GOOD

Pratt's Bounced Throw Hands Tampa Bay Four Runs Before a Brewer Bats; Milwaukee Files at the Lead All Evening, Frelick Finds Dead Center on the Ninth Pitch of a Battle, and the Rookie's Seventh-Inning Single Buys the Game Back Before 43,245 — Robin Yount Among Them

Baseball's bookkeeping permits a man to repay by nightfall the debt he contracts at dusk, and Cooper Pratt, 22 years old and playing his first World's Series, settled his in full. His bounced throw on Yandy Díaz's leadoff grounder opened the gate, and before Logan Henderson could shut it the Rays had built a 4-0 lead — Chandler Simpson and Junior Caminero cashing singles, then Liam Hicks lifting a two-run drive over the wall in right-center, the first home run this World's Series has seen — four runs in five batters against a starter who had never in his major-league life allowed more than three earned in a game.4 And waiting behind that lead stood Drew Rasmussen, the Tampa Bay ace, with the Series apparently about to be evened.

Milwaukee's answer was the one it has given all October: not the haymaker but the file. In the home first Jonathan Aranda let a catchable foul pop fall untouched beside the screen, and William Contreras, reprieved, lined a single past the second baseman to score Jackson Chourio; Garrett Mitchell's knock brought Jake Bauers across before the inning closed, and the four-run mountain was already half quarried.4 In the fourth Aranda let David Hamilton's grounder through his legs — Pratt, of all men, scoring the run — and Rasmussen, handed the kind of cushion that wins championships, could not keep it: six hits and three runs in 3 2/3 innings, gone before the midpoint with the lead cut to 4-3.

The tying blow came from the least likely bat on the premises. Sal Frelick, owner of four home runs all season and a .614 on-base-plus-slugging, opened the sixth against the left-hander Ian Seymour and simply refused to be put away, fouling off fastball after fastball until the ninth pitch of the argument caught too much plate — and he drove it over the barrier in dead center, his first home run since July 11 and only the fourth of his career against left-handed pitching.7 An inning later Brice Turang doubled, Pratt lined a single to right to fetch him home, and the evening's accounts were squared: the error's author had supplied the deciding run of a 5-4 game. Abner Uribe took the victory, and Aaron Ashby closed it with a five-out save, the last of them a full-count check swing from Díaz that the first-base umpire called, and the batter later conceded.6

So Milwaukee boards for St. Petersburg two games to none to the good, two wins from the first championship in franchise history, and the arithmetic now leans heavily: clubs up two games to none in a best-of-seven have taken the series 80 times in 96, and no club has climbed out of that hole in a World's Series in 30 years, since the 1996 Yankees.3 In the stands sat the 71-year-old who played shortstop the last time this franchise got this far. "Hey, I waited 44 years for this!" said Robin Yount, who has adopted the rookie Pratt as a favorite. "I am not missing a game."3 The third game goes Monday at eight o'clock Eastern under the Tropicana roof, Freddy Peralta against Robert Gasser.8

News Around the League

THE FUNDAMENTALS DESK: THE CLUB OF EIGHT-AND-NINETY WINS BUILT ON THE LITTLE THINGS KEEPS GETTING THE LITTLE THINGS WRONG — A FOUL POP DROPPED, A GROUNDER THROUGH THE LEGS, A RUNNER WAVED INTO AN OUT AT HOME, AND CAMINERO ON HIS FEET IN THE DUGOUT DEMANDING OUTS

The Rays spent six months proving that tidiness wins ballgames, and two October evenings discovering the price of its absence. Saturday's inventory of the uncharacteristic ran long: Aranda's dropped foul pop that re-opened the first inning, and his fourth-inning error that he judged himself without appeal — "I didn't read the spin off the bat well... It was a play that I could have made"; Simpson, in the sixth, unable to secure Christian Yelich's single cleanly; and in the same inning the third-base coach Brady Williams waving Hicks around on Victor Mesa Jr.'s two-out single, whereupon Chourio gathered the ball in shallow left and threw him out at the plate by a comfortable margin on two hops. The manager Kevin Cash stood by the wave — two outs, he reasoned, against a staff that rarely grants three singles in sequence — but summarized the evening without varnish: "Today was probably not our best day."4

The sharpest voice belonged to the young third baseman. Television found Junior Caminero after the sixth shouting at his teammates in the dugout, and he made no apology for it afterward: "We had to get outs. In that moment, we weren't doing our job, and against Milwaukee, if you give up outs, they're gonna do that. They're gonna use that against you." This paper's Larceny Desk wrote Saturday that the stop sign demonstrably exists; the ledger now shows outs surrendered on the bases two nights running, while Milwaukee stole five bags of its own Saturday. Caminero's arithmetic for the remainder was unsentimental — the games left, he said, "are mandatory that we've got to win" — and his timetable brisk: "I already forgot about these last two days. The series now, in my mind, starts on Monday."5 The club's own season offers the precedent: 25 wins in 39 one-run games, and a pennant round in which it shook off a deficit to win three straight.48

THE FIREMAN DESK: FIVE OUTS FRIDAY, FIVE MORE SATURDAY, AND STILL NOT A RUN ON HIS OCTOBER LEDGER — ASHBY PASSES GOSSAGE WITH FIFTEEN SCORELESS INNINGS AND TWO-THIRDS, AND ENDS THE GAME ON A CHECK SWING THE BATTER HIMSELF CONCEDED BY MIDNIGHT

While American Family Field came apart around him, the man who ended the game walked off the mound as though leaving a library. Aaron Ashby's five-out save Saturday — one night after five outs of relief in the opener — ran his scoreless streak to open this postseason to 15 2/3 innings, past Rich Gossage's 1981 and Andy Hawkins' 1984 on the all-time roll; only Andrew Miller, with 16 scoreless to begin the October of 2016, stands ahead of him now. His manager reached for the same comparison the record book did — "It's Goose Gossage-like," said Pat Murphy, before amending upward: "It's been incredible. He does what it takes."6

The ninth tested the calm. Handed the ball over the nominal closer Trevor Megill, who stood hot in the bullpen, Ashby allowed Jonny DeLuca a leadoff double, retired Mesa and the pinch-hitter Ben Williamson as the runner worked to third, and then treated Díaz — one of Tampa Bay's best left-handed bats — with the care of a man defusing something: a stolen strike at the top of the zone, three changeups below it, an unexpected curve into the zone at 3-1, and at full count another curve in the dirt that Díaz could not quite hold off. He dropped his bat and started for first; the first-base umpire James Hoye punched him out; the game was over, twice-checked. By midnight the batter had conceded the call: "In the moment, yeah, I disagreed. The umpire said it was a swing. It is what it is."6

The serenity, Ashby allows, was purchased dearly — shoulder surgery in 2023, an 8.04 earned-run figure back at Triple-A in 2024, a demotion to the bullpen, and some Octobers best forgotten. "It's a lot of breathing," he explained. "Just kind of praying for peace, I guess." Asked whether the composure extends to all quarters of his life, the fireman permitted himself a smile: "Traffic makes me mad sometimes."6

THE GLUE DESK: FOUR HOME RUNS ALL SEASON, AND THEN ONE TO DEAD CENTER IN THE WORLD'S SERIES — NINE PITCHES FROM SEYMOUR, ONE SWING FROM FRELICK, AND A DUGOUT NEAR TEARS OVER THE MAN WHO HOLDS THE MACHINE TOGETHER

Jake Bauers, by his own account, almost wept. Brice Turang could not stop screaming. And the author of the blow just wanted back to the dugout to collect a fist bump from his manager. Sal Frelick's game-tying drive to straightaway center — off a 92.9-mile-an-hour fastball, the ninth pitch of the at-bat — was, by the testimony of everyone in Milwaukee colors, the emotional hinge of the evening, and the reaction was in proportion to its unlikelihood. "I've never seen him hit a dead-center homer in BP," said Bauers. "So to see him do it in a World Series game, I couldn't be happier for him."7

The man himself has made a career of the other virtues. "Murph jokes with me," Frelick said of his manager. "He says I can't hit the ball off the ground to center because it'll be an out the rest of my life. So I was just pumped to try to get back to the dugout so I could give him a big fist bump." Murphy, for his part, had spent the afternoon comparing Frelick's edge to that of Dustin Pedroia, whom he coached in college: "full of a swagger and an edge that, when he went out and played, it was like, 'I'm going to get it done.'" The fullest tribute came from the fireman Ashby: "That was my favorite swing of the year. It's not even close... He's the glue guy. He's the guy that keeps this whole thing together."7

The homer was one of four balls Frelick struck hard on a night Milwaukee ground 184 pitches out of the Tampa Bay staff, and it completed the club's second comeback from four runs down this postseason, alongside the one against Los Angeles in the pennant round — a double feat only four other clubs in postseason history have managed in a single October.7

THE EXILE'S DESK: 'FASTBALL FREDDY' AGAINST THE CLUB THAT RAISED HIM — PERALTA, UNBEATEN SINCE LATE AUGUST, STANDS BETWEEN HIS OLD MATES AND THEIR FIRST CHAMPIONSHIP, AND THE TROPICANA LEDGER SAYS HE IS THE MAN FOR THE WORK

The Series' long parade of reunions saves its starkest for Monday. Freddy Peralta — for years the front of Milwaukee's rotation, dealt to Tampa Bay at the July deadline, and lately the most valuable man of the American pennant round — takes the ball in the third game charged with stopping the very club that made him. The form is formidable: 7-0 with an 0.89 earned-run average over his last ten appearances since August 26, and under the Tropicana roof, where Monday's game will be played, a 1.45 figure with 31 strikeouts across seven starts since the trade. The Rays gave him extra rest after his final pennant-round outing precisely so that their best version of him would meet Milwaukee now; as this paper noted Friday, the alignment was built for this game all along.8

Milwaukee's answer is the left-hander Robert Gasser, who began the season at Triple-A Nashville and pitched his way not merely back but into a World's Series rotation: 2-0 with a 1.51 earned-run average in eight appearances since August 26, the postseason included.8 The histories at stake are plain enough. Of the 57 clubs to lead a World's Series two games to none, 46 have finished the job; against which Tampa Bay can cite its own pennant round, in which it trailed Cleveland and won three straight.8 Milwaukee's faithful, meanwhile, have arranged to attend in absentia: the club sold 31,000 tickets at $15 apiece to watch Monday's road game on the scoreboard at American Family Field — capped so every seat could see the screen — and they were gone in minutes.3

THE AERONAUTICS DESK: THE CREW FLIES SOUTH UNDER FAMILY COLORS — PRIESTER'S UNCLE AT THE CONTROLS OF THE TEAM SHIP, HIS COUSIN IN THE FIRST OFFICER'S CHAIR, AND A HOUSEHOLD OF CONVERTED CHICAGOANS CARRYING THE PENNANT WINNERS TO FLORIDA

The charter that carries Milwaukee to Tampa flies, fittingly, as a family affair. By a report of the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel, the captain of the club's flight south is GJ Priester, uncle of the Brewers right-hander Quinn Priester, with Quinn's cousin Alex seated beside him as first officer — a United Boeing 737 crewed, nose to cabin door, by the pitcher's own blood.9

It is not the elder Priester's first turn with the cargo: he flew the club home from Texas after a series against the Rangers in 2025. The pitcher himself has been grounded since June, when an operation on the thoracic outlet ended his season, and watches the run from the dugout rail; his uncle and cousin, raised just outside Chicago, are described as thoroughly converted to the Milwaukee cause. The Herald notes with approval that a club two wins from its first championship travels in hands with a stake in the matter — and trusts the family to deliver the parcel intact.9

The Series stands two games to none, and the sum of the two margins is two runs — a ledger that reads heavier than its arithmetic, for Milwaukee has now won nine of its ten October games, the last two by coming from behind against the best record in the American League. The particulars ahead are verified and as follows: the third, fourth and fifth games under the Tropicana roof Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday at eight o'clock Eastern, the Series returning to Milwaukee Friday the 30th if required, with the calendar holding a place for a deciding seventh game on Saturday the 31st.2 The paper adds one caution from its own morgue, courtesy of the man in the stands: the 1982 Brewers of Robin Yount led their Series three games to two and never won another game. Nothing is finished at 2-0 — but the club doing the chipping has given no sign it knows how to stop. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
